cells.tense: What you have been building has grown into something that stands without your hand on it
cells.ask: Show one person the structure you have built — not to prove it, just to let them use it.
cells.core:
You kept at this long enough that it became itself. It carries weight now that it couldn't carry before, and the light you've been following is no longer somewhere ahead — it's the ground under you. It shows without you arranging for it to show.

That's the good side: what shines in you comes from finishing something, not from holding something up. The risk here is building past the finish. The frame works. Let someone else stand inside it. Hand one person the shape of what you made, and let their using it be enough, without you standing over it to check it's being used right.
cells.sheetLine: What you built holds on its own now.
cells.verb: Following a light you recognized rather than chose
cells.place: Where you put chaos into a shape that holds

cells.tense: You're living inside the version of this that hasn't happened yet, and it's pushing you
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're trying to get right and leave it exactly as it is for a day.
cells.core:
You're building things in your head that haven't arrived — how this conversation will go, how the plan lands, what they'll need to hear. You're getting there ahead of everyone, laying the structure out before there's anything to hold. That's the excess: the light keeps getting pointed forward, so it dazzles instead of lighting the room you're in.

The good version doesn't need the pitch. You're standing in the light, so people see it; you hold something heavy and stay in contact instead of going hard at it. Pick one thing you're trying to get right and leave it exactly as it is for a day. Let it be unfinished without you.

cells.tense: You planted something once, it never came up, and you stopped expecting anything to
cells.ask: Do one small act of care for something you already started — water it, don't check whether it grew.
cells.core:
Nothing you put in the ground came up. So you stopped putting things in. The work of building structure takes something out of you and you've been running on empty for a while now, hoping that if you just started again it would come out different.

The good version of this grows without forcing. You put something in, you keep the conditions right, you don't grip the outcome. Growth shows up on its own schedule and that doesn't drain you. What's starved isn't the light. Do one small act of care for something you already started — water it, don't check whether it grew. Care that doesn't demand a return is what reaches you now.

cells.tense: You're already lighting the room and describing it as just how the room looks
cells.ask: Name one thing you arranged that others now rely on, and say it was you who built it.
cells.core:
A shape got made and people are standing in it. The order of things, the way the work gets done, the frame everyone moves inside — that came from somewhere, and it came from you. You talk about it like it was already there, or like the room just settled into that shape on its own. It didn't.

The good version of this is knowing your own hand is in what you made. You hold a thing without forcing it, and it contains people rather than crushing them, and you can say so. Name one structure others now depend on, out loud, and say you built it. Not to take credit — to take your own hand back.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft is that the person completes things and receives recognition for it — the record says radiance flows from development that reached completion, but nothing says this person's development actually completed or that anyone noticed. A reader could reasonably say the cultivation happened and no flower came, which is exactly status 3, so I must keep status 1's completion as a condition on the shining rather than a fact about their history. The ask — name the pattern so it can be used by someone else — survives being wrong about which status they are in, because noticing and handing over a structure is useful whether or not the structure is finished. The sentence that serves me more than them is the one about 'your name on it' in the Balanced core; it flatters the writer and I have cut it. The phrase 'the star you steer by' is from the draw and I am rendering it as plain direction rather than quoting the channel vocabulary.
